blueprint.speaker: Dell Hartigan, a retired bookbinder and parent volunteer who has run a monthly book swap at Corbett Hollow Middle School for five years
blueprint.audience: Parents and townspeople of Corbett Hollow who read the community newsletter, including some who watch school board decisions and some who regard the swap as a trivial stopgap
blueprint.exigence: The fifth anniversary of the swap, arriving as the school board prepares to vote again on the library budget
blueprint.purpose: To reframe the swap as a craft with its own lessons, to insist that it is not a substitute for a funded library, and to argue that it teaches children a habit of giving books that will outlast the budget vote
blueprint.context: Six years earlier the district cut the library purchasing allowance and reduced the librarian to part time; the writer began the swap in response
blueprint.claim: The book swap is best understood not as charity or as a replacement for the library but as a craft whose slow practice teaches children to pass books along, a habit that will outlast whichever way the budget vote goes
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Paragraph 1 narrates the first swap and names the thesis (craft, not charity). Paragraph 2 supplies the exigence: the budget cut and its slow effect. Paragraph 3 asks what a swap does and answers with the handling: sorting, mending, keeping a ledger, and the lesson of slowness. Paragraph 4 concedes what the swap cannot do and refuses to let the board use it as an excuse. Paragraph 5 pivots to the one thing the swap does that the library never did: it makes givers of books, illustrated by an anecdote. Paragraph 6 qualifies the scale of the swap, then closes with the antithesis that a craft need not be large to be serious and that the habit will outlast the vote.

devices.function: Opens with a concrete scene of the first swap to establish credibility and the modest scale of the project
Recasts the swap as a craft with tools and lessons, the controlling idea of the essay
Fictional budget figures establish the exigence and the scale of the loss
Compares the stalled library to a town that stops growing, emphasizing gradual, unnoticed decline
The gap as quiet weather conveys a pervasive, unremarked condition
Pivots from context to the essay's analysis of what the swap actually does
Lists the tasks of the craft and the swap's limits, giving concrete texture
Colons set up the specific knowledge the ledger yields and the one thing the swap uniquely does
Very short sentences after long ones enact slowness and create emphasis at the pivot
Parallel short sentences stress the slowness of the craft
Concedes the swap's limits candidly, then pivots to its distinctive benefit
Borrowed versus swapped, returned versus released; large versus serious, rich versus teaching
The boy and the fantasy novel illustrates the claim that swapping makes givers
Pleasure like hearing a letter arrived conveys quiet satisfaction in giving
Limits the scale of the claim before the closing assertion
Modesty, record keeping, and honesty about limits build the writer's credibility
Shifts from candid self-limitation to affirmation
Sets the warning against excusing the board beside the writer's wish to be put out of business

tone_shifts.from: explanatory, somber account of the budget cut
tone_shifts.to: reflective, inquisitive description of the craft

blueprint.counterargument: That a table of secondhand paperbacks is a cheap substitute for a library and could be used by the board as an excuse not to restore funding; the writer concedes the swap's real limits and insists the budget be restored, then argues the swap offers one benefit the library never did

provenance.venue_alias: The Hollow Ledger, a community newsletter
provenance.note: Original reflective essay written for practice-exam use; all names, places and figures are invented.

g-lr41.title: Take One, Leave One
paragraphs: The first swap, five Octobers ago, fit on two folding tables borrowed from the cafeteria at Corbett Hollow Middle School.
I brought forty-one books from my own shelves, most of them paperbacks with cracked spines, and a sign made from the back of a cereal box that said, in marker, Take One, Leave One, No Questions.
By the end of the lunch period the tables held fifty-three books, which is to say the children had done the arithmetic in our favor without being asked.
I have been running the swap every month since, and I have come to think of it less as a charity than as a craft, something with its own tools and its own slow lessons.
The reason the swap exists is not mysterious.

When the district trimmed its budget six years ago, the library's purchasing allowance fell from roughly nine thousand dollars a year to just over one thousand, and the librarian, Mrs. Avendale, went from full time to two days a week.
A thousand dollars buys perhaps sixty new hardcovers, in a building with four hundred and ten students.
The shelves did not empty overnight; they simply stopped growing, the way a town stops growing when the last factory closes and nobody notices until the graduating class is half its old size.
New titles arrived in children's conversations but not in the catalog, and the gap between what they wanted to read and what they could find became a kind of quiet weather in the building.
So what, exactly, does a book swap do that a shelf of donations in the front office does not?
The answer is in the handling.
Every month I sort what comes in, mend what can be mended with linen tape and a bone folder, and set aside what is beyond saving for the art teacher, who turns the pages into collage.
I keep a ledger, a spiral notebook, nothing grand, in which I write down what left the table and what came back.

The ledger has taught me more about the reading life of this town than any survey could: which series travel in packs, which single battered copy has passed through nine households, which eighth grader keeps bringing in horse novels she has outgrown so that someone younger can have them.
Mending is slow.
Sorting is slow.
That slowness is the point, because a craft is a thing you learn by doing it badly for a long time, and the children who help me have learned it alongside me.
I should be honest about what the swap cannot do.
It cannot buy the new book everyone is talking about; it can only wait for someone to tire of it.
It cannot catalog, cannot teach a sixth grader to find a source, cannot do the hundred invisible things Mrs. Avendale does in her two days.
A table of secondhand paperbacks is not a library, and anyone who tells the school board otherwise is handing them an excuse.
I would rather the board restore the budget tomorrow and put me out of business.
And yet.
There is one thing the swap does that the library, even in its funded years, never quite did: it makes children into givers of books rather than only borrowers of them.
A borrowed book is returned because it must be; a swapped book is released because somebody decided another reader should have it.

I have watched a boy stand at the table for most of a lunch period deciding whether he could part with a dog-eared fantasy novel, and I have watched him come back the next month to ask whether anyone took it.
Someone had.
He seemed, if anything, pleased, the way you are pleased to hear that a letter arrived.
I do not want to make the swap sound larger than it is.
It is two tables and a notebook and a roll of linen tape, and on a bad month it is forty books and a rainy lunch period.
But a craft does not have to be large to be serious, and a town does not have to be rich to teach its children that books are things you pass along rather than things you wait to be given.
The budget may come back; I hope it does.
The habit, I suspect, will outlast whichever way the vote goes.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between paragraph 4 and paragraph 5?

options.text: Paragraph 4 states the writer's claim about giving, and paragraph 5 retells that claim through a single narrative example
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The claim about giving appears in paragraph 5 itself, not paragraph 4; paragraph 4 is a concession, not a statement of the claim.

options.text: Paragraph 4 concedes the swap's real limits, and paragraph 5 identifies a distinct benefit that survives those limits
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 4 lists what the swap 'cannot do'; paragraph 5 opens 'And yet' and names 'one thing the swap does that the library... never quite did.'

options.text: Paragraph 4 argues that the budget must be restored, and paragraph 5 supplies the reason the board has resisted doing so
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Paragraph 5 says nothing about the board's reasons; it describes what the swap does for children.

options.text: Paragraph 4 raises objections from the school board, and paragraph 5 refutes each objection with evidence from the ledger
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The limits in paragraph 4 are the writer's own admissions, not the board's objections, and paragraph 5 cites an anecdote, not the ledger.

items.stem: The primary function of paragraph 2 within the passage as a whole is to

options.text: provide evidence that the swap has restored growth to shelves that had stopped expanding
options.label: reversal
options.why: The paragraph describes stalled shelves and a persistent gap; it does not claim the swap reversed the decline.

options.text: introduce the writer's central claim that the swap should be regarded as a craft rather than a charity
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: That claim is introduced at the end of paragraph 1; paragraph 2 provides context, not the thesis.

options.text: argue that the district acted carelessly when it reduced the librarian to two days a week
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The paragraph reports the cut and its effects in a somber tone but does not accuse the district of carelessness or assign blame.

options.text: establish the circumstances that prompted the swap before the writer turns to what the swap actually does
options.label: correct
options.why: The paragraph opens 'The reason the swap exists is not mysterious' and recounts the budget cut and its effects; paragraph 3 then asks what the swap does.

items.stem: The two-word sentence "And yet." at the beginning of paragraph 5 primarily serves to

options.text: condense the concessions of the previous paragraph into a brief summary before the essay's closing section
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The fragment does not summarize; it contrasts with what precedes it and opens a new line of argument, not the conclusion.

options.text: reveal the writer's lingering uncertainty about whether the swap accomplishes anything the library could not
options.label: reversal
options.why: The very next sentence states with confidence that there is 'one thing the swap does' the library never did; the fragment signals assertion, not doubt.

options.text: halt the accumulating list of limitations and mark the writer's turn toward what the swap uniquely offers
options.label: correct
options.why: After four sentences of 'cannot' and a wish to be put out of business, the abrupt fragment pivots to 'one thing the swap does that the library... never quite did.'

options.text: express the writer's growing exasperation with a school board that has ignored repeated requests for funding
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Nothing in the surrounding sentences conveys exasperation; the fragment introduces a quietly affirming claim about children as givers.

items.stem: The primary purpose of paragraph 3 is to

options.text: show that the slow pace of the swap is a weakness the writer has learned to tolerate over five years
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer says 'That slowness is the point,' treating it as the source of the craft's lessons rather than a weakness to be tolerated.

options.text: argue that mending damaged books is more valuable to students than purchasing new hardcovers
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer never ranks mending above buying new books; paragraph 4 explicitly says the swap 'cannot buy the new book everyone is talking about.'

options.text: explain how the ongoing handling of books distinguishes the swap from passive donation and supports calling it a craft
options.label: correct
options.why: The paragraph opens by asking what a swap does that 'a shelf of donations in the front office does not,' answers 'in the handling,' and closes by saying the slowness is the point because 'a craft is a thing you learn by doing it badly for a long time.'

options.text: demonstrate that the ledger provides more reliable data than the district's own surveys of student reading
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The ledger is one of several tasks described, and the comparison to 'any survey' is a passing remark, not the paragraph's organizing purpose.

items.stem: Which of the following best states the overarching thesis of the passage?

options.text: The swap is neither charity nor a replacement for the library but a craft whose slow practice teaches children to pass books along
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 1 frames the swap as 'less a charity than a craft,' paragraph 4 insists it 'is not a library,' and paragraph 6 affirms that the habit of passing books along 'will outlast whichever way the vote goes.'

options.text: The school board must restore the library's purchasing allowance before the swap can accomplish anything lasting
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The writer hopes the budget comes back, but the final sentence says the habit will outlast the vote regardless, so the swap's lasting effect does not depend on restoration.

options.text: Children in a small town will reliably share books if an adult keeps careful records of what they borrow
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The ledger is one tool of the craft, and nothing in the passage attributes the children's giving to the record keeping itself.

options.text: The swap has quietly compensated for the budget cut so effectively that the library's reduced funding no longer harms students
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer explicitly denies this, listing what the swap 'cannot do' and warning that such claims hand the board 'an excuse.'

items.stem: In paragraph 2, the sentence "A thousand dollars buys perhaps sixty new hardcovers, in a building with four hundred and ten students" primarily functions as evidence for which of the following claims?

options.text: The children were willing to contribute more books than they took from the first swap
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: That observation belongs to paragraph 1 and concerns the swap, not the library's purchasing power; the budget figure has no bearing on it.

options.text: Secondhand paperbacks can serve students nearly as well as newly purchased hardcovers
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage makes no comparison of the value of secondhand and new books here; paragraph 4 concedes the swap cannot supply new titles at all.

options.text: The librarian's reduction to two days a week was the most damaging part of the district's decision
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The sentence concerns the purchasing allowance, not staffing hours, and the passage never ranks the two losses against each other.

options.text: The library's collection stopped keeping pace with the needs of its readers after the budget was cut
options.label: correct
options.why: The figure sets the scale of the shortfall and is immediately followed by the claim that the shelves 'simply stopped growing' and that new titles appeared in conversations 'but not in the catalog.'

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the colon in the sentence beginning "There is one thing the swap does that the library, even in its funded years, never quite did" primarily serves to

options.text: signal a shift from the writer's own voice to the reported words of the children at the table
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: No quotation follows the colon; the writer continues in his own voice to state a claim.

options.text: separate two independent observations that the writer considers equally important
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The second part explains and completes the first rather than standing as a separate, parallel observation.

options.text: withhold the distinctive benefit until the end of the sentence so that it lands with emphasis after the buildup
options.label: correct
options.why: The clause before the colon announces that 'one thing' exists without naming it; the colon then delivers 'it makes children into givers of books,' making the claim the focal point.

options.text: introduce a list of several activities that the swap performs more efficiently than the library
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Only a single idea follows the colon, and the writer stresses 'one thing,' not several; nor does the passage claim the swap is more efficient.

items.stem: In paragraph 6, the writer's description of the swap as "two tables and a notebook and a roll of linen tape" is most effective in advancing the argument because it

options.text: makes the modest inventory concrete so that the claim about seriousness that follows cannot be dismissed as exaggeration
options.label: correct
options.why: The plain list follows 'I do not want to make the swap sound larger than it is' and sets up the 'But' sentence that a craft 'does not have to be large to be serious,' so the understatement earns the assertion.

options.text: conveys the writer's frustration that the project has never received the equipment it deserves
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The tone is measured and content, not frustrated; the writer treats the small scale as compatible with seriousness rather than as a grievance.

options.text: catalogs the supplies the board would need to fund if it chose to adopt the swap in place of the library
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer has already rejected the swap as a replacement, and nothing suggests the board is being asked to fund it.

options.text: reminds readers of the first swap in paragraph 1 in order to show how much the project has expanded since then
options.label: reversal
options.why: The list emphasizes that the swap remains small, the opposite of expansion; the writer is deliberately shrinking, not enlarging, its scale.

items.stem: Taken together, the references to "five Octobers ago" in paragraph 1 and to "whichever way the vote goes" in paragraph 6 most strongly suggest that the passage was occasioned by

options.text: a milestone in the life of the swap that happens to coincide with a pending decision about the library budget
options.label: correct
options.why: The opening fixes the swap at five years old and the closing refers to an upcoming vote whose outcome is unknown; the writer reflects on the swap's record at the moment the board is about to decide on funding.

options.text: a recent decision by the school board to cancel the swap in favor of restoring the library budget
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in the passage says the swap is threatened; the writer says the vote has not yet happened and even welcomes being put out of business.

options.text: a dispute with the librarian over whether secondhand paperbacks belong in the school catalog
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Mrs. Avendale is mentioned only with respect, and the writer explicitly says the swap cannot catalog; no dispute appears.

options.text: the writer's announcement that the swap will end now that the budget has finally been restored
options.label: reversal
options.why: Paragraph 6 says the budget 'may come back' and the writer only hopes it does; the restoration has not occurred and the swap is continuing.

items.stem: In paragraph 4, the writer's statement that "anyone who tells the school board otherwise is handing them an excuse" would most likely matter to readers of this passage because it

options.text: acknowledges a worry that the swap could be used to justify leaving the library underfunded, and shows the writer shares it
options.label: correct
options.why: The writer anticipates that townspeople watching the board might fear the swap lets officials off the hook; by naming the danger and asking for the budget to be restored, the writer aligns with that concern.

options.text: criticizes townspeople who have praised the swap too warmly in conversations with members of the board
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The sentence is a caution about an argument, not a rebuke of neighbors; nowhere does the writer say residents have actually made this claim to the board.

options.text: reassures readers that the swap has grown large enough to replace the library's purchasing allowance
options.label: reversal
options.why: The sentence insists on the opposite: a table of paperbacks is not a library, and paragraph 6 stresses how small the swap remains.

options.text: invites readers to pressure Mrs. Avendale to work more days so the swap can focus on mending
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The librarian's reduced hours are a consequence of the cut, not something readers are asked to change; the sentence addresses the board's funding decision.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the phrase "even in its funded years" primarily qualifies the writer's claim about the swap by

options.text: indicating that the benefit described is distinct from the library's mission rather than a consequence of its reduced funding
options.label: correct
options.why: The modifier makes clear the library never produced givers of books even when fully funded, so the swap's contribution is not simply filling a gap the budget cut created and would not vanish if funding returned.

options.text: suggesting that the library accomplished more during its funded years than the writer has previously admitted
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The phrase concedes the library's past strength only in passing; its purpose is to isolate what the library never did, not to expand praise for what it did.

options.text: implying that the budget cut was the reason the library failed to turn children into givers of books
options.label: reversal
options.why: The phrase rules out that explanation by stating the failure held true in the funded years as well.

options.text: conceding that the swap's benefit would disappear once the board restored the purchasing allowance
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: If the library never made givers even when funded, restoring funds would not remove the swap's benefit; the closing paragraph says the habit will outlast the vote.

items.stem: The anecdote about the boy and the "dog-eared fantasy novel" in paragraph 5 most effectively advances the writer's purpose by

options.text: grounding the abstract contrast between returning and releasing a book in a single observed act of deliberate giving
options.label: correct
options.why: The anecdote follows the general distinction in which a swapped book is 'released because somebody decided another reader should have it'; the boy's long deliberation and later question show that decision taking place in a particular child.

options.text: proving that fantasy novels are the series most likely to travel in packs through the town's households
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The ledger observations about series belong to paragraph 3; the anecdote concerns one child's choice, not patterns of circulation.

options.text: demonstrating that the swap's slowness teaches children to mend and sort books alongside the writer
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Mending and sorting are the lesson of paragraph 3; the boy is not shown handling or repairing books, only deciding whether to give one away.

options.text: showing that children feel regret after parting with books and therefore return to reclaim them
options.label: reversal
options.why: The boy returns to ask whether the book was taken and is 'pleased' to learn it was; he does not try to get it back.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the structure of the sentence "A borrowed book is returned because it must be; a swapped book is released because somebody decided another reader should have it" emphasizes the relationship between its ideas by

options.text: repeating the same clause pattern so that the differing verbs and reasons stand out against a matching frame
options.label: correct
options.why: Both halves follow the form 'A ___ book is ___ because ___'; holding the shape constant makes the contrast between 'returned' and 'released' and between obligation and choice the only thing that changes.

options.text: placing the longer clause first so that the shorter one lands as a blunt correction of the reader's assumption
options.label: reversal
options.why: The first clause is the shorter one; the second, about the swapped book, is longer and more elaborated.

options.text: subordinating the idea of borrowing to the idea of swapping to show that one practice causes the other
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The clauses are coordinate, joined by a semicolon, and neither is presented as the cause of the other.

options.text: shifting from passive to active voice to suggest that borrowers act while swappers are acted upon
options.label: reversal
options.why: Both main clauses are passive ('is returned,' 'is released'); the only active verb, 'decided,' belongs to the swapper, the opposite of what this option claims.

blueprint.speaker: Marisol Teague, a cellist who has taught adult students for eleven years at the fictional Pellam Falls Community Music School, writing a first-person feature essay
blueprint.audience: General magazine readers, particularly adults considering taking up an instrument and parents of young music students
blueprint.exigence: The school canceled its spring recital after most adult students who had signed up quietly stopped attending lessons, a pattern the writer has seen every year
blueprint.purpose: To persuade readers that adult learners quit not because they make mistakes but because they interpret mistakes as verdicts on themselves, and to show that teaching can change this interpretation
blueprint.context: A community music school in a small town; adult amateur music instruction; an annual recital cycle from September to spring
blueprint.claim: Learners abandon instruments not because they fail but because they hear each failure as a verdict rather than as information; teachers can and should train students to hear mistakes as messages
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Paragraph 1 establishes the exigence and the puzzle (students leave without failing). Paragraph 2 gives a representative anecdote of a diligent student who quit after one wrong note. Paragraph 3 defines the key distinction between failure as verdict and failure as information. Paragraph 4 concedes that beginners cannot yet read the information in their mistakes, then turns that limitation into a responsibility for teachers. Paragraph 5 describes the writer's Wrong Note Wednesdays practice and its retention results. Paragraph 6 qualifies the claim, then shifts to direct address and closes by restating the verdict/message antithesis.

devices.function: Quantifies the dropout problem and later the retention effect of the Wednesday exercise
The tide simile conveys the inevitability and loss of the annual dropout; the mechanics simile conveys the calm, diagnostic attitude toward error
Ruth's story dramatizes a capable, diligent learner quitting over the interpretation of a single mistake
Very short sentences after longer ones land the key points with blunt emphasis
Legal metaphors (sentence, verdict, plead guilty) and the language metaphor frame the two ways of hearing failure
Explicitly defines failure as verdict versus failure as information
Balanced opposing clauses sharpen the verdict/information distinction
Matching structures make the two interpretations directly comparable
Admits beginners cannot read their mistakes, then reframes this as a reason to teach differently
Colons introduce concrete lists that ground abstract claims in specifics
Lists of specific actions and reasons add concreteness
Limits the claim so the exercise is not oversold
Turns to the reader as prospective learner or parent to apply the argument
Repeated 'verdict' and 'information/message' keep the central distinction before the reader
Establishes the writer's long teaching experience and hands-on practice

tone_shifts.to: direct, urging address to the reader

blueprint.counterargument: Beginners cannot read the information in their mistakes because they lack the skill to diagnose them, so the verdict/information distinction may be useless to those who need it most; the writer concedes the gap but argues it is a reason for teachers to do the translating aloud, not evidence that adults cannot learn

provenance.note: Entirely fictional writer, school, town, students and figures.

g-lr24.title: The Wrong Note Is Not the Verdict
paragraphs: In March the Pellam Falls Community Music School canceled its spring recital, and nobody was surprised except the people who had never taught there.
Of the forty-one adult students who had signed up in September to play a piece in front of an audience, fourteen remained by the first week of March.
The rest had not failed their lessons; most of them had been progressing on schedule.
They had simply stopped coming.
I have taught cello at the school for eleven years, and I have watched this happen every spring, like a tide that goes out and does not come back.
Consider Ruth Abernathy, a retired pharmacist who began lessons at fifty-eight because, as she told me, she was tired of being an audience.
For five months she was my most diligent student: she taped her fingerboard, counted aloud, and arrived early to tune.
Then one Tuesday in February, playing a simple shift from first position to fourth, she landed a half step flat and heard it.
She stopped, lowered the bow, and said, very quietly, "So that is what I sound like."
She did not come back.
The missed note had told her something true about her hand, but she heard it as a sentence passed on her whole person.
That distinction is the one I most want adult learners to understand, so let me draw it plainly.
A failure can be treated as a verdict, a judgment about who you are, or it can be treated as information, a report about what your hand did at a particular moment under particular conditions.
The verdict closes a case; the information opens one.
The verdict asks, "Am I musical?"; the information asks, "Was my elbow too low?"
Professional musicians are not people who have stopped making mistakes; they are people who have learned to hear a wrong note as a question rather than an answer.
I will grant that this is easier to say than to do, and that beginners face a genuine obstacle in doing it.
A flat note carries information only to someone with enough skill to read it, and a beginner, almost by definition, lacks that skill.
Ruth heard that the note was wrong; she could not yet hear why.
In that gap, where the ear is good enough to detect error but not yet good enough to diagnose it, the verdict rushes in to fill the silence.
But the gap is an argument for teaching differently, not an argument that adults cannot learn.
If the student cannot yet translate a mistake into instruction, then for a while the teacher must do the translating out loud, until the student learns the grammar.
Three years ago I began running what my students, not entirely kindly, call Wrong Note Wednesdays.
Once a week, each student plays a passage for the group with the deliberate goal of missing something: a shift, a rhythm, a string crossing.
The group then names what they heard, and the player names what the hand did.
There is no applause and no wincing, only a room full of adults saying "the thumb got left behind" with the calm of mechanics discussing a carburetor.
The exercise is faintly ridiculous, and the students know it.
Yet of the twenty-six students who have passed through the Wednesday group, twenty-two were still enrolled the following autumn, against a school-wide retention rate of roughly half.
They do not play better than the others, at least not at first.
They quit less.
I do not want to overstate what a Wednesday can do.
Some students leave for reasons no exercise can touch: a move, a diagnosis, a grandchild who needs the spare room where the cello lived.
And a practiced ear for one's own mistakes is not the same thing as talent, whatever talent is.

But if you are an adult thinking about picking up an instrument, or a parent watching a child's enthusiasm curdle at the first hard page, I would ask you to notice which kind of failure is on offer in the room.
If every wrong note is a verdict, the learner will eventually plead guilty and leave.
If every wrong note is a message, the learner may stay long enough to become fluent in the language, which is, after all, the only thing we ever meant by learning to play.

items.stem: The writer's portrayal of Ruth Abernathy in paragraph 2 most directly appeals to the audience by

options.text: demonstrating that common beginner habits such as taping the fingerboard and counting aloud are ineffective, so that readers seek more rigorous instruction methods
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The habits are listed to show Ruth's diligence, not to criticize them; the passage never evaluates the methods themselves.

options.text: presenting a diligent, steadily progressing adult whose departure cannot be blamed on effort or ability, so that readers who fear their own mistakes see quitting as a matter of interpretation
options.label: correct
options.why: Ruth is 'my most diligent student,' progressing for five months, and leaves after one flat note heard 'as a sentence passed on her whole person,' which locates the problem in interpretation, not capacity.

options.text: suggesting that adults who begin lessons late in life lack the ear required to distinguish a correct note from an incorrect one, so that readers lower their expectations
options.label: reversal
options.why: Ruth 'heard it' immediately; the passage says her ear detected the error, and the writer explicitly denies that the gap means adults cannot learn.

options.text: evoking sympathy for an older learner humiliated in front of peers, so that readers support the school's decision to cancel public performances like the recital
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Ruth's mistake occurs in a private lesson, no humiliation before peers is described, and the writer never endorses canceling the recital.

items.stem: Which of the following best states the overarching thesis of the passage?

options.text: Professional musicians differ from amateur players chiefly because years of practice have allowed them to stop making audible mistakes during performance
options.label: reversal
options.why: The passage states professionals 'are not people who have stopped making mistakes'; expertise lies in how they hear errors.

options.text: Because beginners cannot yet diagnose the causes of their own errors, adults who start an instrument late are unlikely to persist long enough to become fluent
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer concedes the diagnostic gap but insists it 'is an argument for teaching differently, not an argument that adults cannot learn.'

options.text: Community music schools should replace traditional spring recitals with weekly group sessions in which students perform deliberate errors for one another
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Wrong Note Wednesdays is one illustrative practice in paragraph 5, and the writer explicitly refuses to 'overstate what a Wednesday can do.'

options.text: Adult learners abandon instruments not because they make mistakes but because they hear mistakes as judgments of themselves, a habit that teaching can change
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraphs 1 through 3 establish that students leave without failing and that the verdict/information distinction explains why; paragraphs 4 through 6 argue teachers can train the alternative hearing.

items.stem: In paragraph 4, the writer's admission that the distinction is "easier to say than to do" primarily functions to

options.text: narrow the central claim so that it applies only to students who already possess the ear needed to diagnose their own errors in real time
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Rather than restricting the claim to skilled students, the paragraph extends it to beginners by assigning the diagnostic work to the teacher.

options.text: concede that the verdict-versus-information distinction, while useful to professionals, offers little practical guidance to the adult learners it was meant to help
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The writer admits beginners cannot apply the distinction alone but does not abandon it for them; the teacher supplies the translation 'until the student learns the grammar.'

options.text: acknowledge that beginners cannot yet read the information in their mistakes and then redirect that limitation into a responsibility for teachers
options.label: correct
options.why: The concession (beginners lack the skill to read a flat note) is followed by 'But the gap is an argument for teaching differently' and the demand that teachers translate aloud.

options.text: grant that adults who begin late will usually quit, so that the writer's later proposal appears modest and realistic rather than overly ambitious
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer explicitly rejects the idea that the gap shows 'adults cannot learn.'

items.stem: The primary function of the first paragraph in the passage as a whole is to

options.text: preview the deliberate-mistake exercise that the writer will later recommend as a solution to the dropout problem
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Paragraph 1 contains no hint of Wrong Note Wednesdays, which first appear in paragraph 5.

options.text: establish the occasion for the essay and pose the puzzle that the remaining paragraphs set out to explain
options.label: correct
options.why: The canceled recital and the dropout figures supply the exigence, and the observation that students 'had not failed their lessons' yet 'simply stopped coming' is the puzzle the verdict/information argument resolves.

options.text: criticize the school's administrators for canceling the recital rather than addressing the reasons students were leaving
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer reports the cancellation without blame and says 'nobody was surprised' among those who teach there.

options.text: present the writer's eleven years of teaching as the principal evidence on which the argument about failure will rest
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The teaching experience is a brief credibility note; the argument rests on Ruth's anecdote, the definition, and the Wednesday results.

items.stem: In paragraph 6, the writer's reference to "a parent watching a child's enthusiasm curdle at the first hard page" most directly serves to

options.text: remind readers that the writer's teaching experience includes young students as well as the adults described earlier
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in the passage indicates the writer teaches children; the school's students described are adults, and the parent is addressed as a reader, not as a client.

options.text: extend the argument to readers who are not learners themselves but who shape the conditions in which a learner meets failure
options.label: correct
options.why: The sentence pairs the prospective adult learner with a parent and asks both to notice "which kind of failure is on offer in the room," inviting the parent to apply the verdict/message distinction to a child's experience.

options.text: concede that the Wednesday exercise cannot be adapted for children, whose mistakes carry less information than adults' do
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The sentence is an appeal to the reader, not a concession about the exercise; the concessions in paragraph 6 concern moves, diagnoses, and talent, not children's suitability.

options.text: suggest that children abandon instruments more quickly than adults because they lack the patience to work through hard passages
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage never compares children's and adults' persistence; the parent is addressed as an observer of the child's environment, not as evidence about children's patience.

items.stem: The figures in paragraph 5 concerning the twenty-six students who passed through the Wednesday group are offered primarily as evidence that

options.text: adult learners enjoy an exercise they find ridiculous once they understand its purpose and see its results
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The paragraph says the students find the exercise "faintly ridiculous" and name it "not entirely kindly"; the figures address retention, not enjoyment.

options.text: the school-wide dropout problem described in paragraph 1 has been largely resolved since the exercise was introduced
options.label: too_broad
options.why: The comparison is between the Wednesday group and a school-wide rate of "roughly half," which shows the school-wide problem persists outside the group.

options.text: students who practice hearing mistakes as information become more skillful players than their peers within a year
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer explicitly denies this: "They do not play better than the others, at least not at first." The figures measure enrollment, not skill.

options.text: a deliberate practice of naming errors is associated with students continuing their lessons rather than quitting
options.label: correct
options.why: Twenty-two of twenty-six remained enrolled against a school-wide rate of roughly half, and the paragraph concludes "They quit less," tying the figures to retention.

items.stem: In paragraph 3, the structure of the sentence "Professional musicians are not people who have stopped making mistakes; they are people who have learned to hear a wrong note as a question rather than an answer" primarily emphasizes

options.text: an equal balance between two valid descriptions of expertise, inviting readers to choose the one that fits their experience
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The clauses are not offered as alternatives of equal standing; the first is negated and the second affirmed, so the structure argues rather than invites choice.

options.text: the writer's reluctance to define what a professional musician is, since the sentence offers only what such a musician is not
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The first clause is a negation, but the second clause supplies a positive definition, so the sentence does define the professional rather than avoiding it.

options.text: a correction of a likely assumption, replacing a definition based on flawless playing with one based on how mistakes are heard
options.label: correct
options.why: The parallel clauses, "are not people who... ; they are people who...," first reject the expected standard (no mistakes) and then substitute the writer's standard (hearing a wrong note as a question), making the contrast the point.

options.text: that professionals differ from beginners mainly in the number of wrong notes they produce during a performance
options.label: reversal
options.why: The first clause explicitly denies that professionals have stopped making mistakes; the sentence locates the difference in interpretation, not frequency.

items.stem: In paragraph 6, the colon in the sentence "Some students leave for reasons no exercise can touch: a move, a diagnosis, a grandchild who needs the spare room where the cello lived" is effective primarily because it

options.text: marks the point where the paragraph turns from qualifying the argument to addressing the reader directly as a prospective learner
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The turn to direct address occurs two sentences later with "But if you are an adult"; the colon sentence is still within the qualification.

options.text: introduces concrete particulars that make the preceding general concession credible and humane rather than merely dutiful
options.label: correct
options.why: The clause before the colon states an abstract limit on the exercise; the items after it, ending with the grandchild and the spare room, give that limit specific weight, so the concession reads as genuinely felt.

options.text: creates suspense about which of the three reasons the writer considers most responsible for the school's dropout rate
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The list is not ranked and the writer draws no conclusion about which reason dominates; the point is that none of these reasons can be addressed by the exercise.

options.text: separates the writer's own reasons for leaving teaching from the reasons the students give, clarifying whose experience is described
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer has not left teaching and gives no personal reasons; both halves of the sentence concern students.

items.stem: In paragraph 4, the sentence "Ruth heard that the note was wrong; she could not yet hear why" is best understood as evidence supporting which of the following claims?

options.text: Beginners possess enough skill to detect their errors but not enough to diagnose them.
options.label: correct
options.why: The sentence directly follows the claim that 'A flat note carries information only to someone with enough skill to read it' and illustrates the 'gap' described next, where the ear detects error but cannot diagnose it.

options.text: Diligent practice habits do not protect adult students from quitting after a single mistake.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: That idea belongs to the anecdote in paragraph 2; in paragraph 4 Ruth is reintroduced to illustrate the skill gap, not her diligence or departure.

options.text: Adults who begin lessons late in life are unlikely ever to learn to read their own mistakes.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The paragraph explicitly rejects this reading: the gap 'is an argument for teaching differently, not an argument that adults cannot learn,' and the word 'yet' signals that the skill can still come.

options.text: Teachers must translate a student's mistakes aloud until the student can do so independently.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: This is the conclusion the writer draws at the end of paragraph 4, not the claim the Ruth sentence directly supports; the sentence illustrates the problem (the gap), and the teaching remedy follows from it later.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between paragraph 4 and paragraph 5?

options.text: Paragraph 4 concludes that teachers must voice the meaning of mistakes for students; paragraph 5 describes a practice the writer built to do exactly that.
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 4 ends with 'the teacher must do the translating out loud,' and paragraph 5 opens with the writer's Wrong Note Wednesdays, in which the group names what it heard and the player names what the hand did.

options.text: Paragraph 4 argues that adult beginners face an obstacle no teaching can remove; paragraph 5 offers evidence that the obstacle is smaller than it appears.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Paragraph 4 explicitly says the gap 'is an argument for teaching differently,' not an immovable obstacle, so paragraph 5 does not contradict paragraph 4 but carries out its conclusion.

options.text: Paragraph 4 presents the writer's theory of how learners interpret failure; paragraph 5 restates that theory in the words of the students themselves.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The theory of verdict versus information is defined in paragraph 3, not paragraph 4, and paragraph 5 reports a practice and its retention results rather than restating a theory.

options.text: Paragraph 4 raises doubts about whether the verdict and information distinction matters; paragraph 5 sets those doubts aside by returning to Ruth's story.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Paragraph 4 never doubts that the distinction matters, only that beginners can apply it unaided, and paragraph 5 does not return to Ruth at all.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the comparison of the students to "mechanics discussing a carburetor" primarily advances the writer's purpose by

options.text: portraying error analysis as a neutral, technical task rather than an occasion for shame or praise.
options.label: correct
options.why: The simile follows 'There is no applause and no wincing' and attaches the 'calm' of mechanics to adults naming what the hand did, modeling failure heard as information rather than verdict.

options.text: suggesting that adult learners bring workplace habits to music that younger students lack.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in the passage contrasts adults with children on the basis of professional habits; the comparison is about the attitude in the room, not the students' backgrounds.

options.text: conceding that the Wednesday exercise reduces music to a mechanical routine with little artistry.
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: The word 'mechanics' invites this misreading, but the simile praises the calm, diagnostic stance; the writer's only concession about the exercise is that it is 'faintly ridiculous,' which comes in the next sentence.

options.text: demonstrating that students who diagnose their own errors quickly outplay those who do not.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer states the opposite: 'They do not play better than the others, at least not at first. They quit less.'

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the phrases "not entirely kindly" and "faintly ridiculous" are most effective in the argument because they

options.text: admit the exercise's awkwardness before the retention figures, so the results appear credible rather than oversold.
options.label: correct
options.why: The self-deprecating diction concedes the exercise looks silly and that students mock its name; the following 'Yet' then introduces the figures, making the writer seem candid and the results harder to dismiss.

options.text: signal that the writer has grown disillusioned with the exercise despite its initial promise.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The tone is wry, not disillusioned; the writer continues running the exercise and immediately cites its strong retention results.

options.text: mock the students for failing to appreciate a practice that the writer regards as serious.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The mild mockery is aimed at the exercise and, by extension, the writer; the students' good-natured teasing is reported approvingly, and 'the students know it' aligns them with the writer.

options.text: establish that the writer's authority rests on humor rather than on years of experience.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The writer's authority has already been grounded in eleven years of teaching and three years of running the group; the humor softens that authority but does not replace it.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the writer's shift from the past tense of "Three years ago I began running" to the present tense in "each student plays a passage for the group" primarily serves to

options.text: present the exercise as a continuing routine rather than a single remembered event.
options.label: correct
options.why: After dating the exercise's origin, the present tense ('plays,' 'names,' 'There is no applause') describes what happens 'Once a week,' casting the practice as ongoing, in contrast with the one-time past-tense account of Ruth in paragraph 2.

options.text: indicate that the writer is now describing a hypothetical lesson rather than one that occurred.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The paragraph reports a real weekly practice with actual enrollment figures; nothing marks the scene as hypothetical.

options.text: mark the point at which the writer stops narrating and begins addressing the reader directly.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Direct address to the reader ('if you are an adult') does not begin until paragraph 6; paragraph 5 remains third-person description of the students.

options.text: emphasize that the students, not the teacher, now control how the sessions are conducted.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The present tense covers the whole routine, including the group's and the player's roles; it says nothing about who controls the sessions, and the writer remains the one running them.

blueprint.purpose: To persuade garden members to approve a signal booster and study table at the garden shed so students without home internet can do homework
blueprint.audience: Members of the Hollis Creek Community Garden, many of them retired growers who care about cost and the plots, voting at the November meeting
blueprint.claim: The garden can cheaply and responsibly help close the homework gap for ridge families by improving the shed's Wi-Fi and adding a study space
blueprint.theme: rural broadband and the homework gap

planned_flaws.flaw: Vague thesis that neither requires proof nor previews the proposal
Insulting tone toward the very readers being asked to vote
Cost stated without addressing members' budget concerns
Missing transition signaling an additional proposal
Missing transition from objection to response
Does not acknowledge older members who studied without internet

provenance.venue_alias: Hollis Creek Community Garden bulletin board

g-lw41.title: Homework at the Garden Fence
paragraphs: Every Thursday evening this fall, a few cars have been parked along the fence of the Hollis Creek Community Garden with their engines off and their dome lights on.
Inside them are kids from up on Marrow Ridge doing homework, because the weak Wi-Fi from the garden shed reaches the gravel lot and their houses get no signal at all.
Internet is important for students these days.
My name is Tessa Lindqvist, and I was one of those kids last spring.
Our teachers post every assignment online, and the county's math program will not even load on a phone showing one bar.
My neighbor's son, Caleb, failed a chemistry quiz because the practice set timed out four times on his mother's hotspot.
Obviously, anyone who doesn't get this is clueless about how school works now.
The garden committee could fix part of this problem cheaply.
A signal booster mounted on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars, according to the hardware co-op in Pell.
A picnic table under the shed awning, with one outdoor outlet, would let students work somewhere other than a cold car.
The garden already stays open until dusk, so no new hours would be needed.
Some members worry that teenagers will trample the beds or leave trash behind.
Students using the table would agree to stay by the shed and to pick up before leaving each night.
I am asking every member to vote yes at the November 9 meeting.

items.stem: Many garden members are retirees who keep a close eye on the committee's small budget. The writer wants to revise sentence 9 to address this audience's concern about cost. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: A signal booster on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars, which is honestly nothing compared to what a good education is worth.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Dismisses the members' budget worry instead of addressing it.

options.text: A signal booster on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars, less than last summer's new hoses, and my family has offered to pay half.
options.label: correct
options.why: Puts the cost in terms members know and reduces the burden on the budget, directly answering their concern.

options.text: A signal booster on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars, and it would probably pay for itself many times over someday.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Makes a vague, unsupported financial claim that does not reassure budget-minded readers.

options.text: A signal booster on the shed roof, a model with two antennas and a weatherproof case, is sold at the hardware co-op in Pell.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Adds product details but drops the cost entirely, ignoring the audience's concern.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 5 that respects members who finished school without the internet while explaining why students today cannot do the same. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Today the assignments exist only online, and the school stopped handing out printed packets two years ago.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Explains the change but does not acknowledge members who studied without the internet.

options.text: Many of you did homework with a library book and a pencil, which shows that the old way was always better for kids.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Undercuts the writer's own argument instead of explaining why students now need internet.

options.text: Many of you probably think kids today are lazy and just want to sit on their phones at the garden fence.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Assumes the worst of readers rather than respecting them, and explains nothing.

options.text: Many of you did homework with a library book and a pencil, but today the assignments themselves exist only online.
options.label: correct
options.why: Honors members' experience and explains the change that makes their approach impossible now.

items.stem: The writer wants to begin sentence 10 with a transition that signals a second, separate improvement following the one described in sentence 9. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: For instance,
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Presents the table as an example of the booster, which it is not.

options.text: In contrast,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Signals opposition, but the table complements the booster.

options.text: As a result,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Wrongly implies the booster causes the table to exist.

options.text: In addition,
options.label: correct
options.why: Signals that the table is a further improvement added to the booster.

items.stem: The writer wants to begin sentence 13 with a transition that shows the sentence is a response to the worry raised in sentence 12. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Similarly to that concern,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Signals likeness, but sentence 13 answers rather than resembles the worry.

options.text: To address that concern,
options.label: correct
options.why: Directly marks sentence 13 as the answer to the members' worry.

options.text: Despite that small concern,
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Belittles the members' worry and suggests the writer will disregard it.

options.text: Because of that concern,
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Mentions the concern but frames the promise as merely caused by it, not as a reply.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 14 that ends the flyer by reminding garden members that the proposal fits values they already hold as growers. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: If the vote fails, students will keep failing quizzes like Caleb did, and the committee will have to explain why it let that happen.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Ends on a threat that blames the readers instead of appealing to their values.

options.text: The signal booster from the co-op in Pell can be installed in about an afternoon by any member who owns a sturdy ladder.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Gives a practical detail rather than a closing appeal to shared values.

options.text: High-speed internet is now a basic need across the country, and every rural community will have to deal with the gap sooner or later.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Moves away from this garden and its members' values to a general national claim.

options.text: This garden has always shared its extra seedlings and spare tools with neighbors, and a table and a stronger signal would just be one more thing we share.
options.label: correct
options.why: Ties the proposal to the members' existing habit of sharing, so the ending appeals to values they already hold.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 6 that explains how Caleb's experience supports the claim that students need a reliable connection. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Chemistry is widely considered one of the hardest subjects in high school, especially for students who struggle with math.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Suggests the subject was the problem, which works against the point about the connection.

options.text: His mother has since switched to a different phone plan, though the hotspot still drops out when it rains on the ridge.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Mentions the connection again but does not explain how the example supports the claim.

options.text: He knew the material, but a weak signal kept him from practicing it, so the connection decided his grade more than his effort did.
options.label: correct
options.why: Explains how the anecdote shows that unreliable access, not ability, hurt his grade.

options.text: Caleb is a junior this year and hopes to study nursing at a college somewhere in the state after he graduates.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Adds background about Caleb that has nothing to do with the claim.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 3 with a thesis that makes an arguable claim and previews the proposal that the rest of the flyer develops. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: For a small cost and with clear rules, the garden can give these students a better signal and a real place to work.
options.label: correct
options.why: Takes a position members could dispute and previews the cost, the booster and table, and the rules discussed in paragraphs 3 and 4.

options.text: Many rural families across the country still struggle to get a dependable internet connection at home.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: States a general fact that needs no argument and never mentions the garden's proposal.

options.text: A signal booster on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars from the hardware co-op in Pell.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Gives one detail from paragraph 3 and leaves out the study table and the response to members' worries.

options.text: Students on Marrow Ridge have been sitting in parked cars by the garden fence every Thursday this fall.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Repeats the scene from sentences 1 and 2 and makes no claim that would need proof.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 11 so that it admits a limit of the proposal without dropping the point that the garden's schedule would not have to change. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The garden already stays open until dusk, so no new hours would be needed, though in November dusk comes early enough that students would still have to finish some work elsewhere.
options.label: correct
options.why: Keeps the claim about hours and honestly notes that early dusk limits how much the table can help.

options.text: The garden already stays open until dusk, so no new hours would be needed, and the table would give students all the study time they could ever need.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Makes the claim even bigger instead of admitting a limit.

options.text: The garden already stays open until dusk, but the committee should probably add evening hours, staffed by volunteers, so students can stay as late as they want to.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Admits a limit but drops the point that no schedule change is needed, which hurts the low-cost case.

options.text: The garden already stays open until dusk, which most members agree is the best time of day to water seedlings and check the tomato beds for pests.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Wanders into gardening chores and never qualifies the claim about students.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 7 with a sentence that keeps the point about how school has changed while using a respectful tone toward the garden members being asked to vote. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Many of us finished school with only textbooks, but for today's students, an assignment that won't load is an assignment that can't be done.
options.label: correct
options.why: Respects members' own experience and still makes the point that schoolwork now depends on a connection.

options.text: Members who still think kids can get by with library books seriously need to catch up with the times.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Still talks down to the readers whose votes the writer needs.

options.text: School is probably a little different now, though honestly it may not matter very much to anyone here.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Polite, but it undercuts the argument by saying the problem may not matter.

options.text: It is truly heartbreaking that innocent children are being utterly abandoned by an uncaring world.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The overblown, melodramatic wording doesn't suit a practical flyer and blames people unfairly.

blueprint.purpose: To show college admissions readers how working at a public pool shaped the writer's sense of civic responsibility
blueprint.claim: A public pool is a rare place where strangers become neighbors, and keeping such a place open takes people who will speak up for it.
blueprint.theme: public swimming pools as shared civic spaces

planned_flaws.flaw: Claim needs more specific evidence that strangers actually connect
Slangy tone unsuited to admissions readers

g-lw44.title: Forty Lengths at Harrow Street
paragraphs: Every summer since I was fourteen, I have spent my mornings at the Harrow Street Pool in Calder Falls, first as a swimmer and now as a lifeguard.
Pools are important to communities in many ways.
At six in the morning, the lap lanes belong to retirees like Mr. Okafor, who swims exactly forty lengths and then tells me the water temperature as if I had not measured it myself.
By noon, the shallow end fills with day-camp kids whose counselors call out names in four languages.
The pool brings together people who would never otherwise meet.
Last July, I watched a retired machinist teach a nine-year-old girl from the apartments on Delmont Avenue how to float on her back, his hand flat beneath her spine until she no longer needed it.
Last spring, the city council proposed closing Harrow Street to save money.
Everyone in town agreed that this was a terrible idea.
I spoke at the budget hearing, holding a petition with 312 signatures I had collected at the snack bar.
The council kept the pool open, but it cut the evening hours, the only time many working parents could bring their children.
That decision was totally lame, and honestly it bugged me a lot.

What I learned from all of this is that the thing I learned is that a public space only stays public if the people who use it are willing to show up and speak up for it in the places where the decisions about it get made.
In conclusion, swimming is a very good form of exercise for people of all ages.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 13 with a conclusion that connects her experience at the pool to the kind of member she hopes to be in a college community. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Swimming at Harrow Street kept me healthy for years, and I plan to keep doing laps at whatever college pool I find next fall.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Focuses on exercise, not on civic engagement or community membership.

options.text: Public spaces of every kind, from parks to libraries to plazas, are the foundation of any healthy democratic society in the world.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Generalizes about society without connecting to the writer or college.

options.text: Wherever I go next, I want to be the one who knows the regulars by name and shows up at the meeting when their shared space is at risk.
options.label: correct
options.why: Links the pool lessons (knowing regulars, speaking up) to her future role in a new community.

options.text: Next summer I hope to earn my advanced lifeguard certification, which requires sixty hours of training and a timed rescue test.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Introduces a new, unrelated detail instead of concluding the essay's argument.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 6 that provides further evidence for the claim in sentence 5 that the pool connects people who would otherwise never meet. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The girl practiced floating every afternoon after that, and by August she could swim the full width of the pool alone.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Follows the girl's progress but says nothing about a connection between people.

options.text: That summer the pool recorded more than nine thousand visits, its highest attendance since the snack bar was renovated.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Attendance shows popularity, not that strangers formed connections.

options.text: Most people agree that a cool pool is one of the most relaxing places to spend a hot afternoon in the middle of July.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: A vague generalization unrelated to people meeting.

options.text: Neither knew the other's name when the lesson began, and by August her mother was bringing him tomatoes from their balcony garden.
options.label: correct
options.why: Shows two strangers from different backgrounds forming an ongoing connection through the pool.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 11 so that it conveys her frustration in a tone appropriate for college admissions readers. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The decision frustrated me, because the families who most needed the pool had lost the only hours they could use it.
options.label: correct
options.why: Expresses frustration in measured, mature language and gives a reason.

options.text: That decision represented an unconscionable betrayal of every citizen, a wound upon the very soul of Calder Falls.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Melodramatic and inflated rather than sincere.

options.text: The decision was a total disaster, and it made me so mad that I could barely stand to look at the council members.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Remains overly emotional and informal for admissions readers.

options.text: The decision reduced operational hours by approximately three per day, effective at the start of the fiscal year.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Clinical and detached; drops the frustration entirely.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 2 so that it gives college admissions readers, who look for personal reflection, a clear sense of what the pool came to mean to her. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Honestly, the pool is basically the best spot in Calder Falls, and everybody knows it.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Uses casual, boastful phrasing and an unsupported claim instead of thoughtful reflection.

options.text: Lifeguards must be certified in first aid and must renew that certification every two years.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Gives a procedural fact that has nothing to do with the essay's reflective claim.

options.text: Public pools across the country offer recreation, safety training, and relief from summer heat.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Makes a general statement about pools nationwide and leaves out the writer's own reflection.

options.text: Over those summers, I came to see the pool as one of the few places in town where strangers become neighbors.
options.label: correct
options.why: Offers a personal insight drawn from her experience and previews the essay's claim, which is what admissions readers look for.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 10 that explains how the council's decision weakens the role she says the pool plays in the community. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The council also discussed repaving Delmont Avenue and repainting the library that night.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Moves to unrelated agenda items rather than commenting on the pool decision.

options.text: Even so, the pool stayed open, so the petition clearly achieved everything it set out to do.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Says the outcome was a full success, which goes against the writer's point that the cut did real harm.

options.text: Without those hours, the families who most needed a shared place to meet their neighbors were the ones left out.
options.label: correct
options.why: Links the lost evening hours to the claim that the pool brings strangers together, showing who is now cut off.

options.text: The evening lifeguards were reassigned to the morning shift, which was already fully staffed.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Adds a staffing detail that has no basis in the draft and does not explain the effect on the community.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 12 so that it is concise and states her lesson without repetition. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: I learned that public spaces matter to everyone in many different ways.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Concise, but it loses the specific point about showing up where decisions are made.

options.text: I learned that a public space stays public, so its users show up wherever decisions are made.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: "So" reverses the condition and makes it sound as if staying public causes people to show up.

options.text: What I learned is that the lesson I learned is that public spaces need people to speak up for them.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Shortens the sentence but keeps the redundant "learned" construction.

options.text: I learned that a public space stays public only if its users show up and speak up where decisions are made.
options.label: correct
options.why: Removes the repeated "I learned" and the wordy phrasing but keeps the full lesson.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 7 so that college admissions readers, who have never been to Calder Falls, understand why closing Harrow Street would matter to the people she described in paragraph 2. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Last spring, the city council proposed closing Harrow Street, the only public pool within walking distance of Delmont Avenue, to save money.
options.label: correct
options.why: It gives outside readers one concrete detail about the stakes and ties it to the neighborhood of the girl in sentence 6, so the threat feels real.

options.text: Last spring, the city council, which meets on the second floor of the old library, proposed closing Harrow Street to save money.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The detail describes where the council meets, not why the pool matters to the people who use it.

options.text: Last spring, the city council proposed closing Harrow Street to save money, which, believe me, was a seriously big deal for us.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: It is casual and only says the closing mattered. It never shows readers why.

options.text: Last spring, the city council proposed closing Harrow Street, the most important pool in the entire state, to save money.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: It makes an inflated claim that nothing in the essay supports, and it does not explain what the pool means to local residents.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence at the end of paragraph 1 that states a thesis needing proof and previews both halves of the essay: the pool bringing people together and the fight to keep it open. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Those mornings taught me that a pool can turn strangers into neighbors, and that it stays open only if someone will stand up for it.
options.label: correct
options.why: It makes an arguable claim and points ahead to paragraph 2 (strangers connecting) and paragraph 3 (speaking at the hearing).

options.text: Those mornings taught me that a pool can turn strangers into neighbors, from retirees in the lap lanes to campers in the shallow end.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: It previews only the community half and leaves out the civic fight in paragraph 3.

options.text: Those mornings taught me that every public space in every town shapes the character of the citizens who happen to use it.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: It is too sweeping for what one essay can prove, and it previews neither the pool's specific role nor the hearing.

options.text: Those mornings started at six o'clock, and I have worked at the pool for several summers, first swimming and later guarding.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: It repeats facts from sentence 1 and makes no claim, so it cannot serve as a thesis.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 6 so that it begins with a phrase describing the machinist standing in the water, and the phrase must clearly and correctly modify him. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Standing waist-deep beside her last July, a retired machinist taught a nine-year-old girl from Delmont Avenue to float on her back.
options.label: correct
options.why: The opening phrase sits right next to the noun it describes, the machinist, so the modifier is placed correctly.

options.text: Standing waist-deep beside her last July, a nine-year-old girl from Delmont Avenue was taught to float by a retired machinist.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: This is a misplaced modifier: the phrase seems to describe the girl, not the machinist.

options.text: Standing waist-deep beside her last July, I watched a retired machinist teach a nine-year-old girl from Delmont Avenue to float.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: The phrase now attaches to the narrator, not to the machinist the writer meant to describe.

options.text: Standing waist-deep beside her last July; a retired machinist taught a nine-year-old girl from Delmont Avenue to float on her back.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The modifier is in the right place, but the semicolon wrongly cuts the phrase off from the main clause.

items.stem: The writer wants to begin sentence 10 with a transition showing that her speech at the hearing helped lead to the council's decision but did not fully succeed. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Partly because of that hearing, the council kept the pool open,
options.label: correct
options.why: 'Partly because of' shows a limited cause-and-effect link, which fits a result that was only a partial victory.

options.text: Despite everything said at the hearing, the council kept the pool open,
options.label: reversal
options.why: It suggests the hearing worked against the result, which reverses the link the writer intends.

options.text: For example, at the end of the hearing, the council kept the pool open,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Sentence 10 is not an example of sentence 9, so 'For example' signals the wrong relationship.

options.text: Entirely because of my petition, the council kept the pool open,
options.label: unsupported
options.why: It claims full credit, which the essay does not support, and it hides the partial nature of the outcome.
